title: Living in the IT Era
text:
This page contains lecture notes, exercises, and supplementary material for Living in the IT Era, prepared primarily for the first-year BS Biology students whom I teach. The course is not intended to turn students into computer technicians or make them memorise catalogues of devices, inventors, and fashionable technologies. Its purpose is to provide enough working knowledge to make better decisions about computers, internet services, software, privacy, security, online conduct, AI, and other technologies that students encounter in ordinary life and scientific work.
Much of the subject will already be familiar in fragments. A student may know one part from using a phone, another from connecting to Wi-Fi, and another from hearing about online scams or AI. The course brings those pieces together, fills important gaps, and explains how they are related. Examples are drawn whenever practicable from biology, health, research, and Philippine digital life.
The module follows the broad general-education scope described for Living in the IT Era in CHED Memorandum Order No. 20, series of 2013. Its ten-chapter plan is a modern interpretation of that scope rather than a claim that CHED prescribes this exact sequence. The notes will be developed as the course proceeds and may change in response to students’ questions, suggestions, and practical needs.

title: Living in the IT Era
text:
How classes will work
We shall use a flipped-classroom approach. Students first encounter the assigned material by reading the announced pages or sections before class. Class meetings will provide a bird’s-eye view of the chapter and concentrate on questions, discussion, examples, and practical applications rather than repeat the notes line by line.
The assigned reading will not usually be terribly long, and students are not expected to master it before class. They are, however, expected to read the assigned sections carefully rather than skim only the headings and examples. They should arrive familiar with the main ideas and ready to say what was clear, what was confusing, and what deserves further discussion. Reading before class is part of the course rather than optional preparation for it.

title: Living in the IT Era
text:
House rules

“…The young must be idealistic; the young must believe that the world should be more just, and there should be more moral rectitude in the behaviour of their leaders… (But) at the end of the day I think decisions have got to be made by adults, not teenagers. But it’s got to be made in such a way that when the teenagers become adults, and they look back on these decisions, they would be proud of the generation that went before them.” — Lee Kuan Yew


Printed notes are available if you need them. If you do not have reliable access to a laptop or mobile device, speak to me after class or during consultation hours. You do not need to explain your circumstances; I will provide the relevant printed material free of charge.
Attend regularly and arrive on time. Much of the course depends on discussion, questions, and guided work that cannot be reconstructed fully from the notes. The notes are a guide rather than a transcript, and the examples or pace may change. Any change affecting examinable material will be announced clearly.
Complete the announced reading before class. Unlike the advance reading for MMW, the MST reading should not be treated as a quick skim. Read the assigned sections carefully from beginning to end. If you encounter an unfamiliar term, make a brief effort to look it up using a search engine or dependable reference. This does not require a full research project; the aim is simply to understand enough to follow the discussion and identify what still needs explanation. Bring those questions, examples from your own experience, and claims that you would like the class to examine.
Participate and ask for help. Questions are welcome in class, by email, and during consultation hours. You will not be judged if a technical idea is difficult or unfamiliar. Ask classmates, compare notes, and speak to me when something remains unclear.






NoteLanguage in our classroom



The notes use British English. The differences between British and American English are relatively subtle in this course, apart from some spelling conventions and a few terms, so they should not cause difficulty. Either is acceptable if your meaning is clear and consistent. English is useful for reading technical and biological literature, but it is not a barrier to participation. Students may use any dialect of Tagalog or Cebuano, or English. If my accent or wording is difficult to follow, tell me; I can explain in Taglish whenever practicable.


Discuss ideas firmly but civilly. A useful discussion may involve disagreement. Address the claim rather than embarrassing the person who made it, distinguish evidence from opinion, and be willing to correct or revise a position. The same standard applies to communication in class and online.
Use devices and generative AI thoughtfully. A phone or laptop may be a legitimate tool for reading, checking a specification, examining a source, or recording a question. Use it for the work at hand without distracting other people. Generative-AI tools may offer explanations or alternative perspectives, but fluent answers can still be wrong. Check important claims against the notes and dependable sources, and do not use AI during a graded assessment unless I have expressly permitted it.
Protect other people’s information. Do not share a classmate’s personal details, messages, photographs, recordings, account information, or screenshots without permission. Use fictitious or properly anonymised data when an activity does not require real personal information.
Help improve the course. Please point out factual errors, unclear explanations, broken links, and practical topics that the notes have overlooked. Correct mistakes respectfully. The notes are being developed alongside the course, and well-founded student feedback may shape later versions.

title: Exorcising a Demon I: From Manila to London
text:
The London skyline at dusk, viewed across Tower Bridge and the River Thames.



“He who has a why to live for can bear almost any how.” — Friedrich Nietzsche

Four years ago, I decided to leave public life at what was probably the height of my career. After nearly a decade as a professional content creator, I felt it was time to move on and pursue other interests.
I had spent years in the political firing line, taking figurative bullets for what I believed was right—whether I was right or mistaken. I was also getting older, and it had become clear that I needed to start looking after myself because no one else was going to do it for me.
Fiery opinion writing was never on my bingo card when I was younger. Fresh out of secondary school, I enrolled at the University of the Philippines Diliman to study mathematics. Things went well for a time—I believe I was among the strongest students in my class—until life intervened. Suffice it to say that the financial difficulties my family faced after my father’s death set off a chain of events that eventually forced me to leave university at the age of eighteen.
I was something of a lost soul for much of my twenties, and it took me a long time to recover. The recovery was never complete, but life gradually became more manageable. For better or worse, I eventually found myself in the political arena, where I remained for eight years.
Two presidential elections later, however, I realised that I was getting older and that an old inner demon still needed exorcising.
In a culture that places an almost sacred value on education, the fact that I had never completed my degree haunted me endlessly. At thirty-seven, I decided it was time to take another shot at it and, once and for all, lay that ghost to rest. I needed to finish my mathematics degree.
In my mind, returning to a Philippine university was no longer an option. I assumed that my chequered academic record, together with the public profile created by my subsequent political career, would make me an impossible prospect for any admissions panel. I wanted to begin again abroad, far from the political noise that had followed me for years.
So I looked overseas.
I knew that my circumstances were unusual and that my academic credentials were nearly two decades old. I applied to foreign universities with the private understanding that the whole exercise was a moonshot. I must have applied to more than a hundred institutions. After more than a hundred rejection letters, four eventually offered me a place.
The first was for Finance and Investment at the University of Kent in south-east England. The second was for Applied Mathematics and Statistics at SUNY Korea in Incheon. The third was for Commerce at the University of Canterbury in Christchurch, New Zealand. The fourth was for Economics at the University of York in northern England.
Of the four, York felt like the best fit for me, so I accepted its offer.
There was, however, a catch. Before beginning my first year, I had to complete a year-long international foundation programme. My academic qualifications were simply too old to be accepted at face value, and York wanted proof that I was ready to return to formal study.
I looked into my options and found what seemed like a shortcut: Kaplan International College London offered an intensive six-month foundation programme that could lead to York.
So I took it. I did not care that I would end up studying economics rather than mathematics. I was simply grateful to have been given a chance at a new life.
My first day at college in London brought its own private humiliation. I was in my late thirties, while most of my classmates were quite literally two decades younger than I was. They could have been my own children. I was even older than some of my teachers. No one treated me differently, but I still found it embarrassing to walk into the classroom each day, feeling that I had entered a place meant for the young, not merely the young at heart.
Still, I was paying for the whole thing with money I had earned from content creation. I had no choice but to swallow my pride and study as hard as I could.
By the third month, after the midterm examinations, I was among the top students in my class. Mathematics had made the difference. It had always been my first love, and it turned out that, despite everything, it had not entirely forgotten me.
While considering what to do next, I discovered that Kaplan London also sent students to the University of Bristol. More importantly, Bristol offered the subject I had wanted to return to all along: mathematics.
My confidence, however, had not recovered as quickly as my ambition. I was not yet prepared to stake everything on a degree in mathematics alone, so I chose Mathematics and Economics instead. It was partly a hedge: economics would still involve considerable abstraction and quantitative work, but I hoped that the broader combination might be a little kinder to me if mathematics proved overwhelming.
I applied to change pathways, and the college agreed—but on the condition that my required progression mark be raised.
It was a considerable risk. If I failed, I would return to Manila not merely as someone who had dropped out of university once, but as someone who had done so both in the Philippines and abroad.

title: Exorcising a Demon IV: The NHS, Wimbledon, Bristol, and Filipino Psychology
text:
← Previous post: Exorcising a Demon III: From Bristol to Bristol
Before explaining just how wrong I was about my final-year project, I need to take a detour. Rereading the first three parts of this series, I noticed that I had moved from paranoid defeatism to cautious optimism without losing the habit of making jokes at my own expense. The little bit of Britain I had acquired thought, good grief, this sounds like a soap opera. A restrained Englishman might have said that university had been “a bit difficult” and left it there.
Perhaps there is some melodrama in them, but the Filipino heart was doing most of the talking. My family, friends and lecturers were not supporting characters in an individual story; they were part of how I understood myself. Perhaps it was only then that I began to see the people at Bristol as kapwa, rather than as potential judges.

title: Exorcising a Demon IV: The NHS, Wimbledon, Bristol, and Filipino Psychology
section: Filipino Nurses and a Tennis Player
text:
Filipino Nurses and a Tennis Player
That is why this detour begins in an NHS hospital ward. Most of us will need a nurse eventually, and Britain has a horde of Filipino nurses. One of them may well be caring for you. Their care may feel unusually personal: more patient than the circumstances reasonably permit or more concerned about your comfort than the job strictly requires.
This is not a theorem about Filipino nurses. A population of more than a hundred million people will provide counterexamples to almost any proposition. I am interested in the narrower question of why some Filipino nurses appear to treat care as something more personal than a professional transaction.
To understand that, consider Alex Eala. Her ranking bears her name, and she wins or loses her own matches. Yet Filipinos fill courts wherever she plays. They queued for hours at Wimbledon and followed her to Washington, where she won her first tour-level WTA title. The Philippines, which is not known as a tennis country, promptly developed several million experts on second serves.
After her Wimbledon run, President Ferdinand Marcos Jr received her at Malacañan Palace and praised the way she carried her Filipino identity onto the court. Eala has said much the same thing herself: where she comes from forms part of who she is. She competes on an individual professional tour, yet Filipinos experience her victories as partly theirs.

title: Exorcising a Demon IV: The NHS, Wimbledon, Bristol, and Filipino Psychology
text:
The Audience in My Head
I understand this because something similar happened inside my head at Bristol. There was no flag beside my name on an examination paper, but I worried that my performance reflected upon Filipinos generally. If I struggled, I felt that I was confirming somebody’s doubts about us; if I did well, I felt that I had defended a national reputation nobody had asked me to defend.
My lecturers had imposed none of this. They could distinguish one Filipino with a chequered academic history from an entire country. If I failed Linear Algebra, nobody was going to summon the Philippine ambassador. The audience was largely imaginary, but that did not make it harmless.
Virgilio Enriquez’s concept of kapwa helps explain it. Enriquez, the founder of Sikolohiyang Pilipino, argued that Filipino psychology should begin with Filipino language and experience rather than assume that concepts developed elsewhere would fit us perfectly.
Kapwa is sometimes translated as “other person”, although that loses much of its meaning. In English, the other is separate from me. With kapwa, the other person and I share something of the same identity. This does not mean Filipinos live in perpetual harmony; anyone who has attended a Filipino family gathering will know better. It means that the boundary between what belongs to me and what belongs to others is not always absolute. For better or worse, kapwa forms part of our cultural firmware.
I had encountered this when I left content creation. I had around two million followers, most of whom were Filipino, and many felt betrayed when I left public life to return to university. They did not want me to remain stupid; they had simply come to regard my political work as something we shared, so my departure did not appear to be an entirely private decision.
Looking back, I suspect they understood my departure through kapwa. I was trying to finish the education I had abandoned; they saw me walking away from something in which they had also invested. I cannot blame them, but leaving was something I had to do. The work bore my name without belonging only to me.

title: Exorcising a Demon IV: The NHS, Wimbledon, Bristol, and Filipino Psychology
text:
Back to the Ward
The same idea may help us understand your Filipino NHS nurse. I am not a nurse, and using retinal images in a mathematics project does not qualify me to speak for one. I suspect, however, that kapwa explains part of what patients sometimes experience as unusually personal care.
A patient may begin as a stranger but remains kapwa: another person whose suffering is not entirely separate from one’s own. There is also pakikiramdam, the effort to notice what another person feels without waiting for a formal request. The nurse is unlikely to think, “I shall now demonstrate Filipino culture to Bed 12.” They may simply find it difficult to walk away while somebody remains frightened or uncomfortable.
Professional training, experience and temperament still matter. Kapwa is not a complete explanation, but it helps explain why care may feel personal even when the relationship began as a professional one.
There is also a danger. Describing Filipinos as naturally caring, selfless and hardworking gives an overstretched health service a convenient excuse for expecting too much from them. A study of Filipino nurses in Britain noted that, during the first two months of the COVID-19 pandemic, Filipinos were estimated to account for 36 per cent of known healthcare-worker deaths despite comprising about 8 per cent of the NHS nursing workforce. Being good at caring for other people does not make somebody indestructible.
Eala should be allowed to lose without feeling that she has failed the Philippines. I should have been able to perform badly in an examination without treating it as an international incident. A Filipino nurse should be able to finish a shift without believing that exhaustion represents a failure to care.
Kapwa is not the demon that needs exorcising. It fills tennis courts for a young woman from Quezon City, helped the son of a pig farmer and grandson of a rice farmer survive at a university half a planet away, and can make a frightened patient feel that somebody sees them. The demon is the belief that belonging must always be earned through achievement and sacrifice.
If a Filipino nurse cares for you, say thank you, but do not mistake that kindness for an unlimited resource. Kapwa may help explain why they care; it does not mean they do not need caring for.
As for my final-year project, that particular disaster will have to wait.

title: Exorcising a Demon III: From Bristol to Bristol
text:
← Previous post: Exorcising a Demon II: From London to Bristol



The Fry Building, home of the University of Bristol’s School of Mathematics, photographed as I walked there from the School of Economics.



“When the soul suffers too much, it develops a taste for misfortune.” — Albert Camus, The First Man

By the time Year 2 began, I had largely adjusted to a university system that was starkly different from the one I had known in the Philippines. For most of Year 1, I had felt like a fish out of water.
The most difficult adjustment had been the marking system. When I studied mathematics at UP Diliman, final examinations accounted for about 30 per cent of the final mark; most of the remainder came from substantial tests held throughout the term. At Bristol, by contrast, 80 to 90 per cent of the mark in many modules came from the final examination. In short, it was very much a make-or-break affair: an entire term’s work could depend on how well you performed during a few hours in an examination hall.
That comparison needs one qualification. I first entered UP Diliman in 2001—a full quarter of a century before I wrote this, and long before senior high school became part of Philippine basic education. The material I covered during my two years there was therefore roughly comparable in scope to A-level study in England. I had technically been a university student, but I had not yet progressed very far into university-level mathematics.
I also initially found it odd that bachelor’s degrees in England usually last three years rather than the four that are more common in the Philippines and the United States. It began to make more sense when I realised that English degrees are generally much more specialised. They typically include far fewer broad general education requirements than American or Philippine degrees. If you are studying single-honours mathematics, almost all your modules are mathematics. It can be quite heavy.
That was very much on my mind when I left the joint Mathematics and Economics programme for single-honours Mathematics.
For what it is worth, however, I think the English system suited me better. The students around me took their marks seriously, and so did I.
Even so, I studied as though my life depended on it. By then, I had already acclimatised to the local academic culture, so I was no longer as paranoid as I had been in Year 1.
In fact, it was the first time I felt that I had a little spare time. Unfortunately, it was also when I became much more conscious of my age.
University students usually socialise with their classmates. They go on trips, drink in pubs and generally do the things people in their late teens and early twenties are expected to do. I could not quite do the same. My classmates were so much younger than I was that joining them often felt inappropriate, even if nobody else seemed particularly bothered by it. I was always conscious that I was a man approaching forty among students who were barely out of school, and I did not want to put myself in any situation that could be misunderstood.
Truth be told, I am convinced that I was the oldest mathematics undergraduate ever to graduate from Bristol. The next-oldest student I knew was more than a decade younger than I was. I cannot prove the record, but until somebody produces a counterexample, I am keeping the title.
So I remained mostly cooped up in my flat, studying. I had already come too far to risk losing focus. As a result, I had very little social life in Bristol. It was not that I did not want one; I simply felt more comfortable keeping to myself and using the extra time to study.
I kept reminding myself that I had come to England to get a degree. I wanted a social life, but I wanted the degree more.
That did not make the isolation easy. During one meeting with my senior tutor, Dr Skevi Michael, I was telling her how the term had been going when I inadvertently broke down in tears. It was only then, I think, that I fully admitted how lonely the whole experience had become and how often I felt that I was merely pretending I could do mathematics. I sincerely owe her at least half of my degree. Without her advice and support, I might have given up halfway through.
Much of that extra time went into reading the lecture-note PDFs more closely. Some of the proofs were too terse for my brain, so I would take them apart and rewrite them in my own words. I was not trying to improve the originals. I was trying to produce versions that I could actually understand.
I still had serious doubts about my mathematical ability, however, so I would send some of these rewrites to my lecturers and ask whether I had botched them. One of them was Dr Charles Cox, who taught me Linear Algebra. He was remarkably patient and accommodating. He even incorporated some of my rewrites into the official lecture notes and credited me for them.
That gesture meant more to me than he probably realised. It gave my badly damaged mathematical confidence something to hold on to. Perhaps I was not stupid after all.
As Year 2 drew to a close, we were asked to choose our final-year projects—the closest equivalent in my programme to undergraduate theses. We were given around a hundred topics from which to choose. It was only then that I realised quite how large Bristol’s School of Mathematics was.
When my Year 2 marks arrived, my average was much better than it had been in Year 1. By my calculation, an average in the low sixties in Year 3 would be enough for me to graduate with first-class honours.
Still, I could not afford to become complacent. If there is one thing I have learnt over the past four decades, it is that misfortune enjoys dropping by to say hello.
I chose a project advertised as Data and Topology: Persistent Homology. To be perfectly honest, part of the attraction was that it sounded cool. The description listed Linear Algebra or Matrix Algebra as the prerequisite; Metric Spaces might be useful, it said, but was not required. That made the project appear reasonably accessible.
It also helped that the project supervisor was Dr Andrew Donald, one of the coolest lecturers I encountered at Bristol. He had taught me in both Years 1 and 2. He was so chill in class that I sometimes forgot how difficult the mathematics actually was.






NoteA Different World



By then, I had begun to realise that, yes, I was alone, but not quite as alone as I had imagined. For much of the decade before I came to Britain, I had lived in the dog-eat-dog world of politics, where I had grown accustomed to believing that everybody was out to get me and that I had to do everything by myself. I was slow to realise that I no longer lived in that world. Dr Michael, Dr Cox and now Dr Donald showed me that there were people in the School who genuinely wanted to support me. I no longer had to do everything alone. All three also seemed to love what they did, and some of that enthusiasm rubbed off on me. Their support and obvious affection for their work helped keep me sane.


The advert described homology, informally, as counting holes in a space. That caught my attention. In Part I, I wrote that the financial difficulties following my father’s death eventually forced me to leave university. He had suffered from diabetes, and the first serious complication he developed was diabetic retinopathy, a condition that damages the blood vessels of the retina. Suddenly, TDA seemed to offer a way of studying the shapes and structures found in retinal images. It felt as though the project had given me an opportunity to speak to my younger self.
The advert left plenty of room to choose a direction. One could concentrate on the algebraic structures or investigate the shape of particular data sets, with the option of adding a computational element. I ended up doing both: working through the algebraic foundations and then using them to investigate data computationally. I did not want the dissertation to amount to, “Wow, this looks cute—but so what?” I wanted to use persistent homology on a concrete problem, turning patterns in images into something that could be defined, computed and compared.
At the algorithmic level, persistent homology can look like a sequence of matrix reductions. Without the underlying theory, however, the procedure felt uncomfortably hand-wavy. This was algebraic territory, and my algebraic preparation from Years 1 and 2 was much weaker than my background in probability and analysis. The advertised prerequisites were fair; I had simply chosen a direction that demanded rather more from me.
To understand it properly, I had to teach myself elementary algebraic topology from the ground up. I also ended up studying category theory and statistical machine learning—or at least the parts that the project demanded. Suffice it to say that I bade my summer holiday goodbye.
By September 2025, when my final year began, I had already drafted more than half of what would become my dissertation. I had not, however, run a single experiment. My plan was simple: settle the theory first and deal with the application afterwards.
Oh boy, was I wrong.

The illuminated Wills Memorial Building, viewed along Park Street in Bristol at dusk.



“The afternoon knows what the morning never suspected.” — Robert Frost

Faced with an all-consuming fear of utter humiliation, I kept calm and carried on. Well, I carried on, but I was not particularly calm.
I had close to five hours of classes almost every day, and outside those hours, I revised as though the world was about to end. My life in London was monotonous: college, halls, college, halls. Nearly all my spare time was spent studying.
Kaplan’s programme ended in August 2023, while Bristol’s academic year began barely a month later. This created another problem. I had to pay deposits for tuition and accommodation well before September, when I still did not know whether I would actually pass the foundation course. If I failed Kaplan, the whole thing would become a financial disaster.
Somehow, I completed Kaplan’s programme with distinction, which allowed me to progress to Bristol’s BSc Mathematics and Economics programme.
I would have been ecstatic, but there was still much to be done. I had to move to Bristol, a city I had never visited and did not even know how to reach. All I had was Google Maps. With the help of Filipino friends in London, I managed to make the move. After that, all I had to do was wait for the first day of classes.
When that day came, I found myself in exactly the same predicament I had faced in London. My classmates were half my age.
Yes, the private humiliation was still there. But nothing could be done about it. I could blame fate for its wicked sense of humour, or I could shut up and do the work. So I shut up and did the work.
Students entering mathematics degrees in Britain have generally encountered calculus before university. Consequently, my first term already included real analysis: the abstract and rigorous foundations of calculus.
Yes, I had studied calculus at UP Diliman before, but that had been twenty years earlier. I was not even sure whether I could still differentiate anything more complicated than a polynomial.
To make matters worse, I also had linear algebra. Matrices were almost entirely new to me, and I struggled with them so badly that I began to suspect that matrices and I were fundamentally incompatible.
It also did not help that I belatedly discovered that Paul Dirac had studied at Bristol. Yes, the Paul Dirac who helped lay the foundations of quantum mechanics. Winston Churchill had also served as the university’s Chancellor, while several Nobel laureates had studied or worked there. Every new fact I learnt about Bristol made me feel slightly more certain that everybody there was clever except me.
Suffice it to say that my first month in Bristol was pure torture. Was everybody there genuinely brilliant while I was merely pretending to belong?
Almost every day, I wondered whether my return to mathematics was driven by too much ambition and too little talent. I knew that I had shown some aptitude for the subject as a teenager, but that had been a long time ago. I was afraid that whatever mathematical ability I once had might have faded with age.
I wanted to quit, but I could not. By then, I was already in too deep. I had crossed countries, spent much of my savings and reorganised my entire life around this one attempt. I could no longer simply walk away.
I reminded myself that this was my last shot. If I blew it, I would have to wrestle with the same demon until my final breath.
Through sheer force of will, I suppose, I gradually managed to reactivate some long-dormant neurons. I started doing well. Then I started doing very well. The mathematics that had seemed almost impossible during my first few weeks slowly became familiar again.
I began to feel that I could do more. Much more.
This would have been entirely good news, except that my rekindled love for mathematics made me increasingly unhappy with the other half of my degree.
Economics is a beautiful subject, but the mathematics used in first-year undergraduate economics felt too basic for what I had begun to want. I remained optimistic, so I asked the School of Economics whether the mathematics would become more advanced in the later years. They told me that it would eventually reach statistics and linear algebra.
That broke my heart.
I was already studying statistics and linear algebra in my first year. I had hoped that economics would eventually take me far beyond them. Of course, much more advanced mathematics is used in economics, but much of it would not appear until postgraduate study. I did not know whether I would have the time or the money for that. At that point, I did not even know whether I would survive my undergraduate degree.
All I knew was that I loved mathematics, and I intended to make it love me back.
So I contacted the School of Mathematics and asked to transfer from the joint Mathematics and Economics programme to the single-honours Mathematics programme.
They agreed, provided that I finished my first year with a decent upper-second-class average. Very roughly speaking, the required mark occupied the sort of academic territory associated with graduating with honours at a Philippine university, although the two grading systems are not directly equivalent.
I did not have much to lose. If I succeeded, I would be able to study what I really wanted. If I failed, I would simply remain in Mathematics and Economics.
But I wanted mathematics so badly that I barely slept for the rest of the year. I studied all day and often well into the night.
When my final first-year marks came out, I discovered that I had earned a first. I had exceeded the transfer requirement by a considerable margin.
And so, after completing the first year of the BSc Mathematics and Economics programme, I joined the second year of the BSc Mathematics programme.
Things were looking good.
So far.

Hi, I’m Rey Joseph “RJ” Nieto.
I am a mathematician, university instructor, and communications professional. I hold a First Class Honours BSc in Mathematics from the University of Bristol in England and currently teach general-education information technology and mathematics at Bulacan State University (BulSU) in the Philippines. Before returning to formal study, I worked across journalism, broadcasting, public affairs, technical writing, and government communications. title: Mathematics in the Modern World
text:
This page contains lecture notes, examples, exercises, and supplementary material for Mathematics in the Modern World, prepared primarily for the BS Biology students whom I teach. This is not just a mathematics appreciation course. This version of MMW places more emphasis on calculation and mathematical reasoning than students may expect from a general-education course. It may feel challenging at times, but the work is intended to stretch students rather than overwhelm them. This emphasis is consistent with CHED guidelines, which call for students to do mathematics with rigour and apply it to practical problems.
The course has two aims. The first is to develop practical mathematical literacy—including financial literacy—that students can use in everyday life. The second is to introduce a little of several areas of mathematics in preparation for more advanced quantitative courses. Contrary to popular opinion, there is a great deal of mathematics in biology, so examples are drawn whenever possible from biology, ecology, health, and data analysis.
Biological and medical research is highly interdisciplinary. Students are not expected to master every field, but knowing something about different mathematical and computational approaches helps them recognise what a problem calls for—and whom they might ask to collaborate with, whether a statistician, mathematical modeller, computer scientist, or another specialist.
I generally think of this as a challenging but enjoyable course. At a time when so much can feel uncertain, I hope students can find, as I do, some solace in mathematics: definitions can be made clear, assumptions stated, and conclusions followed step by step. Mathematics has easy and difficult parts, just like any other field, but it has acquired an undeservedly nasty reputation. Much of the fear surrounding it begins with that reputation, unfamiliar notation, or an earlier bad experience rather than with the subject itself. It takes practice, but it is not reserved for geniuses. I am not a genius; I learnt mathematics in the same way most people learn anything difficult—by studying, making mistakes, and trying again.

title: Mathematics in the Modern World
text:
House rules

“…The young must be idealistic; the young must believe that the world should be more just, and there should be more moral rectitude in the behaviour of their leaders… (But) at the end of the day I think decisions have got to be made by adults, not teenagers. But it’s got to be made in such a way that when the teenagers become adults, and they look back on these decisions, they would be proud of the generation that went before them.” — Lee Kuan Yew


Printed notes are available if you need them. If you do not have reliable access to a laptop or mobile device, speak to me after class or during consultation hours. You do not need to explain your circumstances; I will provide the relevant printed notes free of charge.
Attend regularly and arrive on time. Much of our learning will happen through explanation, discussion, and guided work in class, and attendance contributes to the final mark under the syllabus and university policy. The notes are a guide rather than a transcript: our pace, examples, and order may change. Any change affecting examinable material will be announced clearly; you will not be assessed on an unannounced topic.
Participate, ask questions, and seek help. Questions are welcome in class, by email, and during consultation hours; longer or off-syllabus discussions are usually best saved for consultation. You will not be judged for finding something difficult. Ask classmates, compare notes, and come to me when something remains unclear. You do not have to struggle alone.






NoteLanguage in our classroom



The notes use British English. The differences between British and American English are relatively subtle in this course, apart from some spelling conventions and a few terms, so they should not cause difficulty. Either is acceptable if your meaning is clear and consistent. Practising English will help with the biology literature, but it is not a barrier to participation. Students may use any dialect of Tagalog or Cebuano, or English. Questions in other languages are also welcome when someone can help translate. If my accent or wording is difficult to follow, tell me—I can explain in Taglish whenever practicable.


Expect biology to involve mathematics. Population growth, inheritance, epidemics, ecological networks, experimental uncertainty, medical images, and protein structures all involve mathematical thinking. You will not be asked to train an artificial neural network; the goal is to recognise quantitative structure, interpret evidence, and reason carefully. These skills matter in biology and medicine as well as in ordinary decisions.






NoteA case in point: mathematics and biology



My BSc Mathematics thesis used computational topology to turn structures in retinal photographs into numerical summaries and test their reliability under changes such as blur, rotation, and noise. It brings together mathematics, computation, and medical imaging. Curious readers can explore the public thesis or the project repository; the advanced mathematics is not required for this course.


Be present and considerate. I have no interest in teaching through fear, and questions are always welcome. In return, help maintain a respectful room: listen when someone is speaking and avoid side conversations. Giving one another our attention makes those “Wow, talaga?” moments much easier to reach.
Bring a notebook and a pen. Record definitions, ideas, examples, and questions in your own words rather than copying everything. After class, practise active recall: reconstruct the main ideas from memory, then check what you missed. Compare notes with classmates and ask me about gaps that remain.






NoteUse of generative AI



Generative-AI tools can provide another explanation, suggest practice questions, or offer a different perspective. Use them cautiously: they can sound convincing while being wrong, so check their claims against the notes and do the mathematics yourself. They cannot replace independent understanding and will not be available during graded assessments.


Work steadily, but keep marks in perspective. Assessments will be proportionate to the available time and published criteria. I will identify enrichment as examinable or non-examinable, and examinations will not hide “curveball” topics whose status was unclear. You may still be asked to apply a familiar idea in a new setting. Quizzes and recitations will be announced and completed in class. Work steadily, and use feedback to improve. Have faith in your ability—I do.
Read the notes before class. I will aim to publish each set of notes at least two weeks before we cover it. You are not expected to master the material beforehand: skim the headings, notice the main ideas and examples, and bring any questions that arise. Mathematics can be difficult, but it becomes more approachable when studied steadily, explained patiently, and connected to meaningful problems.
Correct mistakes—respectfully. Address the idea, never embarrass the person. Please point out errors in the notes or in anything I say; a valid mathematical or factual correction may earn extra credit under criteria applied equally to everyone. Finding a mistake is not a challenge to my authority—it helps improve both the notes and the class, and I will be glad you raised it.
